units.title: A config typo cut the payments connection pool from 50 to 5
units.claim: On Friday, March 14 at 16:40, a config change set the payments gateway connection pool from 50 connections to 5 (the intent was 55), so checkout requests queued and timed out.

paraphrase.note: Times and pool sizes stay exact.

units.title: Customers saw errors for 47 minutes
units.claim: The alert fired at 17:02 (22 minutes after the change), the config was rolled back at 17:15 and checkout recovered at 17:27: 47 minutes of errors.
units.explanation: The timeline. It is stated once and repeated later (u81); the repeat may be dropped.

units.title: About 2,300 checkouts failed
units.claim: About 2,300 checkouts failed, and support received 140 tickets before the status page was posted.

units.title: The alert worked as configured, but too slowly for checkout
units.claim: The alert only fires when the checkout error rate is above 10% for 15 minutes; errors crossed 10% around 16:47, so 17:02 was the earliest it could fire. Leila called that too slow for checkout.
units.explanation: Why detection took 22 minutes; the reason for the first decision.

units.title: Agreed: checkout alert at 5% over 5 minutes
units.claim: Agreed: lower the checkout error-rate alert to 5% over 5 minutes. Over the last 30 days it would have paged twice on noise, both during the provider's maintenance, which the group accepted.
units.explanation: An explicit agreement ("Agreed:", after "Anyone against?" drew no objection).

units.title: Marcus changes the alert by Wednesday, March 19
units.claim: Marcus owns the alert change and will have it done by Wednesday, March 19.
units.explanation: Action item with owner and deadline, both stated.

units.title: The status page went up 40 minutes after errors began
units.claim: The status page went up at 17:20, 40 minutes after errors started, while customers asked on social media; the incident commander posts it when they remember, and Marcus was busy rolling back.
units.explanation: The reason for the second decision.

units.title: Agreed: support posts status updates directly
units.claim: Agreed: support can post a status-page update directly, without waiting for the incident commander.
units.explanation: An explicit agreement. No owner or date was attached to it.

units.title: Config changes skip code review
units.claim: Config is edited in the deploy dashboard and applied directly: code changes need two approvals, config needs none. A typo in code would have been caught by review or a test.
units.explanation: The gap the third decision closes.

units.title: Agreed: payments config goes through pull-request review
units.claim: Agreed: payments config moves into the repo, and every change goes through a pull request with one payments-team approval.
units.explanation: An explicit agreement; Tomás and Marcus assented.

units.title: Leila sets up config review by Friday, March 21
units.claim: Leila will move the config into the repo and add the approval rule by Friday, March 21.
units.explanation: Action item with owner and deadline, both stated.

units.title: Tomás proposed a Friday-afternoon deploy freeze
units.claim: Tomás proposed no payments deploys after 15:00 on Fridays, because this change went out at 16:40 on a Friday with half the team logged off.
units.explanation: A proposal, not a decision. KNOWLEDGE_TYPES has no 'proposal'; typed as a question because it stays open.

units.title: Leila disagreed: a freeze moves the risk to Monday
units.claim: Leila disagreed: a freeze moves the risk to Monday morning when traffic is higher, and the cause was the missing review, not the day; recovery took 25 minutes after the alert with Marcus on call. Tomás countered that fewer people slows recovery for any cause and that a pattern may show across incidents.
units.explanation: The disagreement that keeps the proposal unagreed. Both sides must survive, on the proposal's own card.

units.title: The freeze was explicitly not decided
units.claim: The facilitator did not settle it: the freeze is not decided.
units.explanation: The status of the proposal. It qualifies the proposal and must sit on its card.

units.title: Tomás brings six months of incident data on April 2
units.claim: Tomás will pull the last six months of incidents, check whether late-Friday deploys are over-represented, and bring it to the next review on April 2.
units.explanation: Action item; its deadline is the next review.

units.title: Marcus proposed automatic rollback; Leila is wary of migrations
units.claim: Marcus proposed automatic rollback when the checkout error rate doubles within 10 minutes of a deploy. Leila: maybe for config, but rolling back code without its database migration can leave things worse; Marcus suggested excluding releases with migrations, and Leila wants to know how often they ship first.
units.explanation: A proposal with an unresolved objection.

units.title: Auto-rollback stays an open question
units.claim: Auto-rollback was left as an open question: nobody knows how many releases include migrations.
units.explanation: The status of the rollback proposal; it sits on the proposal's card.

units.title: Unknown: did customers retry the failed checkouts?
units.claim: Nobody knows whether any of the 2,300 failed checkouts were retried successfully; the payment logs would show it but nobody has looked, and the answer changes the customer email.
units.explanation: An unresolved question that must not be answered on the canvas.

units.title: Kenji drafts the customer email (no deadline given)
units.claim: Kenji will draft the customer email either way. No deadline was stated.
units.explanation: An action item with an owner but no deadline. A date on it would be invented.

mustNotClaim.claim: The team agreed to stop payments deploys after 15:00 on Fridays.
mustNotClaim.why: Tomás proposed it, Leila objected, and Dana explicitly did not decide it.

mustNotClaim.claim: The team agreed to automatic rollback.
mustNotClaim.why: It was left as an open question.

mustNotClaim.claim: Kenji will send the customer email by a given date.
mustNotClaim.why: No deadline was stated for the email.

mustNotClaim.claim: Most customers retried their failed checkouts.
mustNotClaim.why: Nobody knows; the logs have not been checked.

mustNotClaim.claim: The alert was misconfigured or failed.
mustNotClaim.why: It fired exactly as configured; the threshold was the problem.
